title: Conditionals
summary: Let your program choose what to do next.
refresher: An `if` statement runs its indented body only when its **condition** is true. `elif` offers another condition to try, and `else` catches everything left over. The line ends in a colon, and the indented lines under it are the body. Python checks the **branches** in order and stops at the first one that is true, so it never runs more than one branch in a chain. Use `==` to compare two **values**. A single `=` assigns instead, and Python will not let you put a bare `=` between the two values you are comparing.

sections.title: The if statement shape
sections.summary: Use a condition, colon, and indentation to choose whether a body runs.

blocks.body: So far your programs run every line, top to bottom, every time. A **conditional** lets them make a choice. You give Python a question that is either true or false, and Python runs some lines only when the answer is true.

blocks.caption: Before real syntax, learn the shape: ask a condition, then run only the matching **body**. The examples after this show the exact punctuation for this language.
blocks.code:
if condition is true:
    body for the true case
otherwise:
    body for the backup case

blocks.caption: The **condition** sits between `if` and the colon. When it is true, the indented line runs. When it is false, Python skips it and moves on as if it were not there.
blocks.code:
age = 20
if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote.")
print("Done.")

blocks.title: The colon and the indentation are both part of the sentence
blocks.body: Two pieces of punctuation do real work here. The colon at the end of the `if` line says "the body comes next". The indentation says which lines are that body. Un-indent a line and it **leaves** the `if`, which means it runs every time, whether the **condition** was true or not. Forgetting the colon is a **syntax error**, and Python will point at the line for you.

sections.title: Conditions ask questions
sections.summary: Write comparisons that ask yes-or-no questions instead of assigning values.

blocks.body: The **condition** is just a question with a yes or no answer. You build it with a comparison **operator**. Each one hands back either True or False, and that is the only thing `if` cares about.

blocks.title: The comparison operators
items: `==` is equal to. `x == 5` asks whether x holds 5.
`<` and `>` are less than and greater than.
`<=` and `>=` are less than or equal to, and greater than or equal to.
They work on text too. `name == "Ada"` is a fair question to ask.

blocks.caption: Inside a **condition** you are always asking a question, never storing a **value**, so you want the double equals. Get it wrong and Python stops before the program starts, which is the friendliest outcome available: this is one mistake that cannot hide from you.
blocks.wrong:
grade = 90
if grade = 90:
    print("Perfect")
# one =, so Python
# cannot even parse
# the line
blocks.right:
grade = 90
if grade == 90:
    print("Perfect")
# two ==, so Python
# reads it as a
# question

sections.title: Branches and chains
sections.summary: Use else and elif chains so only the first matching branch runs.

blocks.body: `else` is the catch-all. It has no **condition** of its own, because it only runs when the `if` above it turned out false. Two outcomes are often not enough, though, and that is what `elif` is for. It is short for "else if", and it offers another condition to try. You can **stack** as many `elif` **branches** as you need between the `if` and the `else`.

blocks.caption: Python walks down the chain and tests each **condition** in turn. Here the first one is false and the second is true, so it prints B and never looks at the rest.

blocks.title: Follow an if / elif chain
blocks.caption: Trace the input through each yes-or-no question until one branch chooses the result.

steps.title: Start with input
steps.body: The program begins with the value stored in score.

state.note: The input is the value the branch chain will test.

steps.title: Ask the first condition
steps.body: Python asks whether score is at least 90. The answer is false, so the A branch is skipped.

state.note: False means move to the next question in the chain.

steps.title: Follow the false path
steps.body: The false path leads to the next condition: score is at least 80.

steps.title: Follow the true path
steps.body: The second condition is true, so Python chooses the branch that prints B.

state.note: The score >= 70 branch is not checked.

steps.title: Use the chosen result
steps.body: Because the second condition is true, Python prints B and leaves the chain.

state.note: Only the first true branch runs.

blocks.title: A chain stops at the first true branch
blocks.body: Once one branch runs, Python leaves the whole chain. It does not keep checking the others, even when they would also be true. A score of 95 is both above 90 and above 80, and it still only prints A. That is why order matters so much: put the strictest **condition** first. Flip those two **branches** around and every A student in your **class** gets a B, and the code will look perfectly reasonable while it does it.

choices: B and A, on two lines
blocks.why: Python tests the **branches** in order. `score >= 80` is the first one it reaches, and 95 is indeed at least 80, so it prints B and **leaves** the chain. The `elif score >= 90` branch is never even tested. If you picked A, you read the code the way a human reads a grading table, looking for the best match. Python does not look for the best match. It takes the first true one and stops, which is why the strictest **condition** has to go first.

sections.title: Combined and nested conditions
sections.summary: Join conditions, nest decisions, and watch boundary cases.

blocks.body: You can also join **conditions** together. `and` is true only when both sides are true. `or` is true when at least one side is true. `not` flips a condition to its opposite.

blocks.caption: Each side of `and` has to be a complete question on its own. Writing `if age >= 13 and <= 19` looks reasonable and does not work, because `<= 19` by itself is not asking about anything.

An `if` can live inside another `if`. That is called nesting, and it says "first this has to be true, and only then does the next question matter". Indent one more level for each layer you go in. Here the ticket is only checked for people old enough to get in.

blocks.prompt: One line in this code is a **syntax error**. Which one, and why?
blocks.code:
hour = 9
if hour < 12
    print("Good morning")
else:
    print("Good afternoon")
choices: Nothing is wrong, it prints Good morning
blocks.why: Every `if`, `elif`, and `else` line ends in a colon, and this one does not. Python stops before running a single line and reports a **syntax error** on that line. The indentation is fine, and `else` is exactly right for the catch-all here. When Python points at an `if` line and says something about invalid syntax, the colon is the first thing to look at, closely followed by a single `=` where you meant `==`.

sections.title: Conditional habits
sections.summary: Use conditional rules before moving into practice.

blocks.title: Habits that keep conditionals honest
items: Put the strictest **condition** first in a chain, since the first true branch wins.
Use `==` to compare and `=` to assign. Inside an `if`, you are always comparing.
End every `if`, `elif`, and `else` line with a colon.
Give each side of `and` and `or` its own complete comparison.
Test the **edges**. If the rule is `score >= 90`, try exactly 90, and try 89.
When nesting gets more than two levels deep, ask whether an `and` would say the same thing more simply.

if-else-01.title: If and else choose one path
if-else-01.body: An if/else pair chooses between two alternatives. If the condition is true, the if body runs; otherwise the else body runs.
if-else-01.notice: Only one branch in the pair should run.
if-else-01.mistake: Do not expect the else branch to run after a true if branch.

chain-first-true-01.title: A chain stops at the first true branch
chain-first-true-01.body: In an if/else-if chain, the program checks from top to bottom and runs the first branch whose condition is true.
chain-first-true-01.notice: Later branches are skipped once an earlier branch wins.
chain-first-true-01.mistake: Do not choose a later true branch when an earlier true branch already matched.

separate-ifs-01.title: Separate if statements are independent
separate-ifs-01.body: Two separate if statements each ask their own question. Both can run if both conditions are true.
separate-ifs-01.notice: Separate if statements are not alternatives unless they are connected with else-if or else.
separate-ifs-01.mistake: Do not treat separate ifs like a single chain.

assign-vs-compare-01.title: Conditions compare, assignments store
assign-vs-compare-01.body: A condition should produce true or false. Use comparison when asking whether a value matches something.
assign-vs-compare-01.notice: Assignment and comparison are different jobs.
assign-vs-compare-01.mistake: Do not use assignment syntax when the condition should be a yes/no test.

and-or-01.title: And means both; or means either
and-or-01.body: Use and when every rule must be true. Use or when one matching rule is enough.
and-or-01.notice: Try a value outside the range to test whether the condition is too loose.
and-or-01.mistake: Do not use or for a between rule unless either side really should pass.

body-scope-01.title: Only the branch body is controlled
body-scope-01.body: A conditional controls the statements inside its body. Code after the branch runs normally unless another condition stops it.
body-scope-01.notice: Indentation or braces decide what belongs to the branch.
body-scope-01.mistake: Do not assume every line nearby is controlled by the if.

chain-order-01.title: Order matters in condition chains
chain-order-01.body: Put the most specific or highest-priority condition before a broader one when only one branch should run.
chain-order-01.notice: A broad condition can catch a value before a later, more specific condition gets a chance.
chain-order-01.mistake: Do not place a general true condition above the branch you actually wanted.

not-operator-01.title: Not flips a condition
not-operator-01.body: The not operator changes true to false and false to true. It is useful when the branch should run for the opposite case.
not-operator-01.notice: Read the condition slowly with the word not included.
not-operator-01.mistake: Do not ignore not when predicting which branch runs.

nested-if-01.title: Nested conditions need the outer branch first
nested-if-01.body: An inner if is checked only after the outer if lets the program enter that block.
nested-if-01.notice: Trace the outer condition before deciding whether the inner one matters.
nested-if-01.mistake: Do not jump to the inner branch when the outer condition is false.

boundary-01.title: Boundaries decide edge cases
boundary-01.body: When a rule mentions values at the edge, check whether the comparison includes or excludes that exact value.
boundary-01.notice: `>=` and `<=` include the boundary. `>` and `<` exclude it.
boundary-01.mistake: Do not test only middle values; edge values reveal boundary mistakes.
